title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: A small UK generator sat offline four days after a cyberattack — government confirms the incident, not the cause
items.content_text: The Sunday Telegraph reported on 22 August that Iran-linked hackers took a British power plant offline for four days. What is actually established is narrower: the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero acknowledges an incident at a small-scale energy generator and says the wider energy system was never at risk. The four-day duration, the Iran attribution and the “unprecedented” framing all rest on the Telegraph’s unnamed officials, and the NCSC would not comment. One detail matters more than the headline — the NCSC received no outage reports from regulated operators, placing the asset below the reporting threshold. That is the exposed population: embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables, typically unmanned and reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router. Alongside the US water intrusions and the S7 advisory, the pressure is landing on the lightly-governed edge.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Sunday Telegraph report, with on-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero — via Irish Times, CNBC, Security Affairs
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement and international pickup 23 Aug 2026; attack reported as occurring in July 2026, exact date not published

items.title: The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through Censys and ZoomEye scanning, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named, across manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A — via CISA, BleepingComputer, Cybersecurity Dive
_otthreatfeed.date_note: AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026, re-verified 23 Aug 2026 morning ET; AA26-097A published 7 Apr 2026, updated 22 Jul 2026; 12-state total through 14 Aug 2026

items.title: Clop’s PLM extortion campaign now names Shell, GE and Philips — the stolen material is plant drawings and blueprints
items.content_text: Clop has listed 43 new victims tied to its exploitation of internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM, the product lifecycle management platforms used across aerospace, defence, automotive, heavy machinery, medtech and retail. On 13 August Shell confirmed it is investigating a “potential incident” after the gang claimed 89 GB of data; on 17 August GE said it is assessing the claim and Philips confirmed a contained compromise of one enterprise server with no customer impact. The gang advertises backups, project plans, facility photographs, drawings, diagrams and blueprints. The entry point is CVE-2026-12569, an input-validation flaw in Windchill and FlexPLM exploited as a zero-day from early June for unauthenticated remote code execution and JSP web-shell deployment. On 18 August ReliaQuest published analysis of the implant itself, and it is not commodity tooling: a Java/JSP web shell written against Windchill’s own internal APIs, database schema, keystore and file-vault layout, with functions for credential access and decryption, repository enumeration, bulk file retrieval and arbitrary Java execution. It was engineered for PLM estates specifically. The detection problem is the part worth carrying into your own environment — the web shell runs as the application’s own service identity, so database telemetry can misattribute the activity as normal application behaviour, and query or file-access logs alone will not separate the theft from ordinary use. PTC began patching on 17 June; CISA added the flaw to KEV on 25 June with a three-day federal remediation deadline. No OT or control-system impact has been reported at any victim — this is confidentiality loss, not disruption. The OT relevance is what was taken: PLM holds the as-designed record of plants, machines and safety systems, and it is rarely inventoried as an OT-adjacent asset or covered by an OT threat model.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Clop leak-site listings and victim statements; implant analysis by ReliaQuest — via BleepingComputer, Computer Weekly
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Victims named 14–17 Aug 2026; GE and Philips responses 17 Aug 2026; web-shell analysis published 18 Aug 2026

items.title: An attacker crossed from a wind farm to a district heating plant through a shared private APN — and stopped a steam turbine
items.content_text: CERT Polska’s follow-up on the December 2025 Polish energy-sector intrusion, disclosed at DEF CON on 9 August and published on 11 August, describes what it calls the first observed case of an attacker reaching an OT network through a private cellular APN. The intruder compromised a FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, used a Teltonika cellular router on that network to enter a private APN operated by the distribution system operator, and from there reached a combined heat and power plant supplying roughly 50,000 residents — an entirely unrelated organisation. A steam turbine and the process-water treatment system were shut down, interrupting cogeneration. Operator response kept it to a short outage with no loss of heat supply. CERT Polska attributes the activity to a Russia-linked actor and notes the root cause was configuration, not exploitation: devices on the shared APN could reach each other freely, a pattern it found was common across Poland.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska follow-up report — via SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Intrusion 29 Dec 2025; disclosed at DEF CON 9 Aug 2026, report published 11 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA put the mass-exploited vCenter flaw in KEV today — and virtualisation is where OT lives now
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-59310 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August, formalising what responders had been reporting for a fortnight. Broadcom published VMSA-2026-0006 on 29 July for the flaw, a directory-traversal issue in the vCenter syslog service rated CVSS 9.8 with no workaround. German incident-response firm QUIRSO observed the first victims connecting to attacker infrastructure on 3 August, five days later; by 5 August roughly 95% of an eventual 361 victim IP addresses across 47 countries had already appeared, concentrated in Germany, the US, Turkey, Iran and France. The actor gains root execution on vCenter, plants a cron job establishing reverse-SSH persistence, and in at least some cases deploys ransomware derived from leaked Babuk source. QUIRSO assesses with moderate confidence that the operator is Chinese-speaking, based on language artefacts in attacker scripts, tooling choices, victimology that excludes mainland China, and working hours consistent with UTC+08:00. No OT or industrial victim has been named. The relevance is structural: HMIs, historians, engineering workstations and SCADA servers increasingly run as guests, so root on vCenter is root on the plant’s supervisory layer.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalogue; Broadcom VMSA-2026-0006 and QUIRSO campaign analysis — via BleepingComputer, Infosecurity Magazine
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Patched 29 Jul 2026; exploitation from 3 Aug 2026; added to CISA KEV 18 Aug 2026

items.title: Ransomware took out door access, elevators and HVAC monitoring at Manitoba’s largest hospital — and a week later they were still restoring it
items.content_text: Shared Health discovered ransomware on the facility-management systems at Winnipeg’s Health Sciences Centre on 10 August, and confirmed in a 17 August update that recovery was still under way across HSC and CancerCare Manitoba. The systems affected were not clinical: central monitoring of heating, ventilation and cooling equipment went dark, door access control and elevators were disrupted, and the site security office could not issue or update staff ID access cards. The plant itself kept running — HVAC equipment stayed operational and was monitored locally at the panels, some exterior entrances were closed or redirected, and Shared Health has said throughout that patient care was not affected and it has no indication patient data was involved. No group has claimed the attack and the initial access vector has not been made public. For OT readers the interest is not the sector but the asset class. Building automation, access control and elevator management are the systems most likely to sit outside both the IT programme and the OT programme — commissioned by facilities or a contractor, remotely supported by that contractor, rarely in the asset inventory, and almost never in the incident response plan. Claroty’s Team82 has been making the same point with data: it found roughly three-quarters of organisations it studied running building management systems carrying known exploited vulnerabilities, with about half of those also insecurely connected to the internet. The consequence here was manual workarounds, degraded monitoring and a hospital that had to fall back on local control and physical processes for a week — the same failure mode a plant would see if its BMS, badge readers and gates went down together during a shift change.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Shared Health statements — via CBC News; supporting BMS exposure data from Claroty Team82
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Attack discovered 10 Aug 2026; Shared Health recovery update 17 Aug 2026

items.title: Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in Q2 — and not one operator touched a control system
items.content_text: Dragos’ second-quarter industrial ransomware analysis records 1,140 victims, up 12% from 1,020 in Q1. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them, 65% of the total; organisations supporting ICS environments accounted for 117 and transportation and logistics for 95. Qilin remained the most active brand, a position it has held since March 2025. The finding that matters for OT teams is the negative one: Dragos observed no ransomware operator directly manipulating an industrial control system during the quarter. Where production stopped, it stopped because enterprise IT was encrypted or because operators pre-emptively shut down virtualisation, identity or remote-access infrastructure that plant systems depended on. Social engineering — increasingly help-desk impersonation inside Microsoft Teams rather than email, walking staff through a screen-share to install remote-access tooling — was the most consistently reported initial-access theme.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Help Net Security
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 11 Aug 2026

items.title: 4,407 Rockwell controllers answer from the public internet — and 22 sit in the exact towns being attacked
items.content_text: An internet-wide scan by Forescout Vedere Labs, published 6 August, found 4,407 internet-facing Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley programmable logic controllers: 65% in the United States, 12% in Canada, 3% in Spain. Twenty-two of them are in cities where water and wastewater utilities have reported cyberattacks since late July, and 19 of those 22 appear vulnerable to CVE-2017-16740, a buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 controllers that Rockwell patched nine years ago. Forescout’s central point reinforces the joint advisory: the effects described publicly — changed IP addresses, set passwords, lost visibility and control — needed no exploit at all, because the controllers were already reachable. Exposure has fallen 47% from a 2020 peak of 7,814, which is real progress and still leaves thousands of directly addressable controllers.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 6 Aug 2026

items.title: A conferencing server handed out a trojanised client to instrumentation and energy firms — and CISA has now put the flaws in KEV
items.content_text: Kaspersky ICS-CERT reported on 12 August that the Head Mare group chained flaws in unpatched TrueConf video-conferencing servers to execute code with SYSTEM privileges, install web shells, and then replace the legitimate Windows client installer held on the server with a trojanised build carrying the PhantomCore and PhantomGraph backdoors. Anyone who took a routine client update from that server was infected — the delivery looked like normal IT housekeeping. Reported victims cluster in instrumentation, electronics, transportation, energy, IT and software firms in Russia and Belarus. On 20 August CISA added two TrueConf Server vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue — CVE-2026-72529, missing authentication for a critical function, and CVE-2026-72530, code injection — which puts the exploitation on the record for everyone else. The transferable lesson is the pattern: a collaboration server sitting in the business zone that also distributes client software is a short, trusted path from IT onto engineering workstations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Kaspersky ICS-CERT report; CISA KEV catalogue addition 20 Aug 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Securelist
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Activity observed Jul 2026; Kaspersky ICS-CERT report published 12 Aug 2026; added to CISA KEV 20 Aug 2026

items.title: The Windows service that terminates a lot of OT vendor VPNs has a pre-authentication RCE — and it is being used
items.content_text: CVE-2026-33824 is a double-free memory-corruption flaw in the Windows IKE Extension, the IKEv2/IPsec service behind Windows Routing and Remote Access VPN endpoints. It allows remote code execution over the network with no authentication and no user interaction — an attacker only needs to reach the IKE listener with a crafted packet. Microsoft shipped the fix in the April 2026 security updates, but exploitation is what changed the priority: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported an operator hand-driving reverse-shell callbacks out of three IKE VPN endpoints, and CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August with a 21 August remediation deadline for federal agencies under BOD 26-04. The OT relevance is the placement, not the product: Windows-hosted IPsec concentrators are a common way integrators, OEMs and remote-support contracts reach plant networks, and a compromised concentrator already sits on the boundary you were relying on.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue; Microsoft security update guide; Unit 42 exploitation reporting
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Patched Apr 2026; added to CISA KEV 18 Aug 2026; BOD 26-04 deadline 21 Aug 2026

items.title: A CVSS 9.5 flaw in the FUXA SCADA/HMI platform lets an unauthenticated attacker write files to the server — scanning began within a day
items.content_text: CVE-2026-25895 is a missing-authentication-plus-path-traversal flaw in FUXA, the open-source web-based SCADA/HMI package used for small automation projects, machine HMIs, remote monitoring and lab or pilot lines. In versions up to and including 1.2.9, a remote attacker with no credentials can write arbitrary files to the server file system and reach remote code execution — and because FUXA typically runs as the process front end, that is code execution on the box operators watch the plant through. VulnCheck reported broad internet scanning for the flaw beginning 18 August, from a single source address attempting to overwrite main.js with junk data; no working RCE payloads have been observed dropped yet, so treat this as reconnaissance ahead of exploitation rather than a confirmed compromise. Roughly 60 FUXA instances answer directly on the public internet. Two other FUXA flaws, CVE-2026-25939 and CVE-2023-33831, remain under active exploitation attempts, the latter with activity traced back to November 2025 and observed again this week — so this is a product already being hunted, not a one-off. Separately, watchTowr reported in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-64849 (CVSS 9.3), an unauthenticated SSRF in the MLflow tracking server, used to pull cloud credentials from metadata endpoints; relevant if your analytics or predictive-maintenance stack runs MLflow alongside plant data. The uncomfortable part of the FUXA story is where these installs live: open-source HMI software rarely appears on an OT asset register, and the people who stood it up are often not the people who patch.
tags: Advisory — SCADA/HMI remote code execution, scanned in the wild

_otthreatfeed.source_name: watchTowr and VulnCheck telemetry; vendor GitHub security advisories — via The Hacker News

items.title: A critical GitLab flaw went from disclosure to in-the-wild exploitation in about two days — and self-managed instances are where control-system projects live
items.content_text: GitLab shipped fixes on 17 August for CVE-2026-19478, a code-injection flaw in its GraphQL API rated CVSS 9.4. An unauthenticated attacker can modify or delete publicly accessible projects and rewrite their state or merge records with a single HTTP request — no credentials, no user interaction, no unusual configuration required. watchTowr reproduced the issue within minutes of the advisory and reported in-the-wild exploitation against its honeypot network roughly two days later. Only self-managed Community and Enterprise Edition installations are affected; the fixed builds are 19.2.4, 19.1.6, 19.0.8 and 18.11.11. The exploitation observed so far is opportunistic and aimed at public projects, and no industrial victim has been named. The reason it belongs on this board is where self-managed GitLab tends to sit in industrial organisations and at their integrators: it is the repository of record for PLC and HMI project files, SCADA and historian configuration, controller firmware images, network drawings, and the pipelines that push all of it toward site. An attacker who can rewrite a repository never has to reach a controller to change what eventually gets loaded onto one, and a repository whose history can be rewritten is no longer a trustworthy source of truth for “what is supposed to be running.” Note also that this is the second item on this board in a fortnight where a general-purpose business server — there a conferencing server handing out client installers, here a source-code platform — sits on a short, trusted path to engineering workstations.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: GitLab security release and vendor advisory; exploitation reported by watchTowr — via The Hacker News, SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Patched 17 Aug 2026; in-the-wild exploitation reported 20–21 Aug 2026

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity unauthenticated RCE in Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050, plus Schneider and Phoenix Contact fixes
items.content_text: Siemens ProductCERT published ten new advisories on 11 August. The one to act on first is SSA-834709: the Node-RED HTTP interface shipped on SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS is missing authentication, so an unauthenticated remote attacker can create flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying system with maximum privileges. Siemens rates it at the top of the scale and has released an updated version. A second critical code-execution flaw was fixed in Siveillance Video Management Servers. Schneider Electric published two advisories covering NetBotz 5 — two code and command execution issues — and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, where a missing limit on authentication attempts was corrected. Phoenix Contact also issued fixes in the same cycle. No exploitation of any of these has been reported.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact — via SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 11 Aug 2026

items.title: Haiwell’s IoT Cloud HMI gateway lets an unauthenticated attacker run OS commands as root
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02, published 13 August, describes an OS command injection flaw in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway. The Net Check feature reachable through the /setting endpoint passes user-supplied input to a cmdPing Socket.io event without sanitisation, so an attacker can inject and execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges. Haiwell has released Scada-v3.50.1.19 to address it. The product is a cloud-connected HMI and remote-access gateway — the class of device that exists precisely to be reachable, which is what makes an unauthenticated root-command flaw in it worth treating as urgent even though no exploitation has been reported. Haiwell equipment is common in smaller integrator-built machine and process installations, where it is often commissioned once and never revisited.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-02
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 13 Aug 2026

items.title: The reissued Medusa advisory puts a number on it: 500+ critical infrastructure victims, and exploits weaponised inside 24 hours
items.content_text: The FBI, CISA and HHS reissued #StopRansomware advisory AA25-071A on 18 August, updating the February 2025 original with investigative findings current to April 2026. The headline count rose from roughly 300 victims to more than 500 across healthcare and public health, the defence industrial base, critical manufacturing, government facilities, information technology and financial services. Two things in the update matter more than the total. The first is speed: the agencies state that Medusa affiliates turn newly disclosed vulnerabilities into working exploits within 24 hours, and in some cases were observed using them before public disclosure — which breaks the assumption behind a 30-day patch cycle for internet-facing kit. The second is the shape of the initial-access list, which the 2026 update extended beyond remote-support and endpoint tooling into managed file transfer and privileged-access appliances: ConnectWise ScreenConnect (CVE-2024-1709), Fortinet FortiClient EMS (CVE-2023-48788), Fortra GoAnywhere MFT (CVE-2025-10035) and BeyondTrust Remote Support / Privileged Remote Access (CVE-2026-1731). Every one of those is a product class that industrial organisations run specifically to let somebody in from outside — integrators, OEM support desks, managed service providers. Post-access tradecraft is the familiar pattern: disable endpoint security, steal data, encrypt broadly, extort twice. No case of hands-on control-system manipulation is described, and none should be inferred; the operational risk here is the same IT-origin production stoppage Dragos documented for the quarter, arriving through the appliance your vendors log in with.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FBI / CISA / HHS #StopRansomware joint advisory, updated release — via BleepingComputer, CyberScoop, Help Net Security
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Original published Mar 2025; updated release published 18 Aug 2026 with findings current to Apr 2026

items.title: Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
items.content_text: Citrix published a bulletin on 19 August covering two flaws in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, and followed it with an unusually direct instruction to upgrade immediately. The serious one is CVE-2026-19490, an authentication bypass a remote attacker can reach without credentials where the appliance runs as an AAA virtual server or as a Gateway — SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy — with exposure depending on firmware version and whether a SAML action is configured. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory-overflow denial-of-service reachable when SIP ALG is enabled on a large-scale NAT group. Citrix has published configuration strings that let you check both preconditions from your own running config rather than guessing from version numbers: look for add authentication samlAction together with add authentication vserver or add vpn vserver for the first, and add lsn group.*sipalg for the second. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32, 13.1-63.21, 14.1-73.32 FIPS and 13.1-37.277 FIPS/NDcPP. SecurAccess ZTNA Hybrid deployments running customer-managed NetScaler instances are in scope too. Neither flaw is reported as exploited yet, and neither is in KEV as of this edition — but the precedent is close and recent: Citrix issued the same kind of warning for CVE-2026-3055 on 23 March, attackers were abusing it within days, and CISA added it to KEV on 30 March with a three-day federal deadline. NetScaler has accumulated 22 KEV entries in five years, six of them used in ransomware. ShadowServer currently sees more than 22,000 NetScaler ADC and roughly 1,800 Gateway instances answering from the internet. For OT owners this is not an ICS advisory and it will not appear in an ICS feed, but it is the box that terminates integrator VPNs, vendor support sessions and engineering-workstation access into the plant — the same class of edge device that carried the intrusions in the Medusa and Polish district-heating cases elsewhere on this page.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — via BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Bulletin published 19 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA’s newest ICS advisory covers a fire-alarm incident manager that keeps passwords and tokens in cleartext in memory
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August, covering CVE-2026-27875 in Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager at version 2.01 and earlier. The application holds user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while running, so an attacker who already has low-privileged local access to the workstation can dump memory, recover those credentials and reach the application and whatever it is connected to. Johnson Controls has released v2.01.01. The severity is genuinely moderate — it needs local access first and there is no reported exploitation — but the deployment is what makes it worth a slot: Simplex Incident Manager is the console operators use to monitor and respond to fire-alarm and life-safety events across a site, and CISA lists it in critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation and energy, deployed worldwide. Life-safety consoles are commonly commissioned by a fire contractor, left on a shared or general-purpose workstation, remotely supported by that contractor, and absent from both the IT and OT asset registers — the same gap the Winnipeg hospital building-automation incident elsewhere on this board exposed from the other direction. Credentials pulled from that console are credentials into the systems that tell you a plant is on fire.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 20 Aug 2026

items.title: Six flaws in Malcolm — the free network-analysis suite a lot of OT shops run as their only passive sensor
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-230-01 on 18 August covering six vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the open-source network traffic analysis suite CISA itself maintains and distributes for ICS and OT environments; the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security reissued it as AV26-841 on 21 August. The affected versions span three release lines — CVE-2026-55676 before 26.06.1; CVE-2026-63133, CVE-2026-63134 and CVE-2026-63177 before 26.07.0; and CVE-2026-19670 and CVE-2026-19671 at or before 26.07.1 — with successful exploitation allowing denial of service or arbitrary code execution. One of the clearer issues is in the archive-extraction path: safe-extract.py unpacked uploaded archives with no cap on entry count, directory depth or output size, so a small crafted archive could drive the Filebeat processing container to create an unbounded number of filesystem objects, exhaust inodes and stall the ingestion pipeline. Release 26.08.0 addresses the set. This one earns its place not on severity but on where it sits. Malcolm is popular precisely because it is free, purpose-built for OT protocols and easy to stand up, which means it is frequently the single passive sensor in plants that have no other visibility — deployed on a span port with broad network reach, run by an engineering team rather than a security team, and patched rarely if ever. A monitoring platform that goes quiet is not just a compromised host; it is the loss of the only record you had of what happened next.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-230-01; Canadian Centre for Cyber Security AV26-841
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 18 Aug 2026; reissued by CCCS 21 Aug 2026

items.title: NERC has to file the expanded internal network monitoring standard by 2 September, and it pulls EACMS and PACS into scope
items.content_text: SERC’s August compliance update sets out the CIP standards currently in flight, and one of them has a date close enough to plan around: NERC must submit a modified CIP-015-2 to FERC by 2 September 2026 extending internal network security monitoring to Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems and Physical Access Control Systems that sit outside the Electronic Security Perimeter. That is a meaningful widening. The first version of the standard concentrated monitoring inside the perimeter, and the systems being added — jump hosts, authentication and access-control infrastructure, badge and door controllers — are exactly the assets an attacker reaches first and the ones that grant onward access to everything else. The update also notes that CIP-003-9 became enforceable on 1 April 2026, that FERC approved the Virtualization Reliability Standards on 19 March 2026 — eleven modified CIP standards plus four new and eighteen modified glossary definitions — and that CIP-002-8 adopts a revised definition of “control center”. Registered entities that categorised assets under the old definitions should expect the scoping exercise to move.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: SERC Reliability Corporation compliance update on approved and pending CIP standards; NERC and FERC filings
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Update published 7 Aug 2026; NERC filing deadline 2 Sep 2026

items.title: The Water Cyber Shield Act would give EPA mandatory-assessment authority and $300M a year for utility cybersecurity
items.content_text: Senators Klobuchar and Schiff introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act on 13 August, three weeks into the multistate PLC campaign. The bill would give EPA authority to require mandatory cybersecurity assessments of water and wastewater systems, direct $300 million a year through the Drinking Water and Clean Water State Revolving Funds for security improvements, and have EPA develop tiered standards in consultation with CISA, NIST, states and sector stakeholders, with additional flexibility and funding priority for smaller systems. It has been introduced, not enacted.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Sens. Klobuchar and Schiff — via WaterWorld, Wastewater Digest
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Introduced 13 Aug 2026
